title: The Tool Nobody Invented
subtitle: The most famous planning tool in the world was taught for decades with the wrong origin story. In 2023, three researchers went looking for the truth.

card.essence: Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats: every business student learns it. But who invented it? For fifty years, the answer everyone repeated had almost no evidence behind it.

intention: you'll learn the detective story behind SWOT, use it to analyse a small business, and practise making guesses about the past: must have, might have, can't have.
warmup: What are your own biggest strengths? Is it easy or hard to say them out loud?
Have you ever believed a “fact” for years and then discovered it was wrong?
Before a big decision, do you make lists of pros and cons? Does it help?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: The old letters were found in a university archive, in a box nobody had opened for sixty years.
items.meaning: archive — a place where historical documents and records are stored.

items.sent: NASA is an acronym for National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
items.meaning: acronym — a word made from the first letters of other words.

items.sent: The famous quotation is often attributed to Einstein, but there is no proof he said it.
items.meaning: attribute (to) — to say that something was written, said or caused by a particular person.

items.sent: In our hurry, we overlooked one important detail: the shop was closed on Mondays.
items.meaning: overlook — to fail to notice or consider something.

vocab.heading: B · Which word matches the meaning?
vocab.intro: The three words are: external · myth · internal. Read each meaning, say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: (noun) A story or belief that many people accept, but which is not true.
items.meaning: myth — “It's a myth that we only use ten per cent of our brains.”

items.sent: (adjective) Inside an organisation, a person or a thing.
(adjective) Coming from outside an organisation, a person or a thing.
items.meaning: external — “Rising oil prices are an external problem we can't control.”

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: hard ___  ·  there is no ___ to support it  ·  give ___ in court
items.meaning: evidence — facts or information that show whether something is true.

items.sent: make a ___  ·  a false ___  ·  ___ to be an expert
items.meaning: claim — to say something is true without proof (verb); a statement of this kind (noun).

items.sent: ___ the origins of a word  ·  ___ a phone call  ·  disappear without ___
items.meaning: trace — to find where something came from (verb); a sign that something existed (noun).

vocab_use: Can you think of a popular myth — about health, history or science — that many people still believe?
Which problems in your job or studies are internal, and which are external?
How far back can you trace your family?

story.heading: Part 1 — The story everyone told
paras: Open almost any business textbook and you will find SWOT analysis: a simple way to look at an organisation's Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats. It is used by companies, charities, schools, hospitals and even students planning their careers. It may be the most widely used planning tool in the world.

For decades, the internet and many books repeated the same origin story. In the 1960s, it said, a management consultant called Albert Humphrey led a big research project at Stanford Research Institute in California, studying hundreds of companies to find out why their planning failed. From that project, the story went, came SWOT.

The story came mainly from Humphrey’s own later account, published in 2005. It was repeated so often that it became accepted as fact. But when researchers looked for evidence from the 1960s — reports, papers, documents with Humphrey's name on the idea — they found almost nothing.
checks: What do the four letters of SWOT stand for?
Who was usually said to have invented SWOT?
What was the problem with this story?
answers: Albert Humphrey, at Stanford Research Institute in the 1960s.
There was almost no evidence from the 1960s to support it; it came mainly from Humphrey's own later account.
story.discuss: Why do you think a story with no evidence was repeated for so long?

story.heading: Part 2 — The detectives
paras: A few years ago, Richard Puyt, a researcher in the Netherlands, became curious. If SWOT was so important, why was its history so unclear? Together with two colleagues, Finn Lie and Celeste Wilderom, he began to dig. They searched archives, read old company reports and interviewed people who had worked at Stanford Research Institute decades earlier.

In 2023, they published what they had found. The idea could be traced back to the 1950s, to planners at the aircraft company Lockheed who were trying to understand why long-range plans so often failed. That work led to Robert F. Stewart, who in 1962 became head of a group at Stanford Research Institute studying the theory and practice of planning.

Stewart's group developed a way of helping managers plan together. It asked them to look at what was Satisfactory, what were Opportunities, what were Faults and what were Threats. The acronym was not SWOT but SOFT, and the institute published the approach in 1965. According to the researchers, Humphrey had been a member of the team — but not its leader, and not the inventor.
checks: How did Puyt and his colleagues search for the truth?
Where could the idea be traced back to?
What was the original acronym, and what did it stand for?
answers: They searched archives, read old company reports and interviewed people who had worked at the institute.
To planners at the aircraft company Lockheed in the 1950s.
story.discuss: Humphrey was a real member of the team. Was his story a lie, a mistake, or something in between?

story.heading: Part 3 — From SOFT to SWOT
paras: Within a few years, the words changed. “Satisfactory” became strengths, and “faults” became weaknesses. SOFT became SWOT, which is easier to say and remember. Around the same time, professors at Harvard Business School were teaching a similar way of thinking: compare a company's internal strengths and weaknesses with the external opportunities and threats around it. The idea spread through business schools and consulting firms until almost everyone used it.

Its simplicity is its strength — and also its weakness. Critics say that many SWOT analyses are just four lists with no decisions. People often overlook the most important question: so what? In 1982, a professor named Heinz Weihrich suggested a fix, the TOWS matrix, which asks how to use each strength to grab an opportunity or defend against a threat.

The story of SWOT has a lesson of its own. Even the world's most famous tools can have a forgotten history, and a fact repeated a thousand times is not necessarily true. Sometimes it takes detectives with patience — and an archive — to find out what really happened.
checks: What is the main criticism of many SWOT analyses?
What does the TOWS matrix add?
answers: They are just four lists with no decisions — they skip the “so what?” question.
It asks how to use strengths to seize opportunities or defend against threats — it turns the lists into strategy.
story.discuss: What other “facts” do people repeat without checking? How could we check them?

tool_tab.lead: SWOT is a checklist in a grid. The top row is internal — things you control. The bottom row is external — things in the world around you. The left column helps your goal; the right column harms it.
how: Write down the goal first. A strength for one goal can be a weakness for another.
Fill the internal boxes honestly: what are we good at, and what do we do badly?
Fill the external boxes: what is changing around us that could help or hurt?
Ask “so what?”: how can each strength grab an opportunity or block a threat? Choose two or three actions.

sort.intro: A small family restaurant has done a SWOT analysis. Which box does each point belong in? Remember: internal or external? Helpful or harmful?

items.text: A large office building with 2,000 workers is opening across the street.
items.why: external and helpful — lots of new lunch customers.

items.text: The chef has won several local cooking awards.
The kitchen equipment is old and often breaks down.
Loyal customers who have eaten there for twenty years.
items.why: internal and helpful — something the restaurant has built.

items.text: A cheap fast-food chain plans to open next door.
Food prices across the country are rising quickly.
items.why: external and harmful — the restaurant can't control it.

breaks: Four lists are not a plan. Without the “so what?” step, SWOT produces pages of notes and no decisions.
No priorities. A tiny weakness and a huge one look the same on the page.
Easy to be too kind to yourself. Teams write long strengths lists and short weaknesses lists.
discuss: Why do people find weaknesses harder to write than strengths?
What would you add to the restaurant's SWOT? What should it do first?

cousins.name: PESTLE
cousins.text: A checklist for the “external” row: political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental.

cousins.name: Porter's Five Forces
cousins.text: Five pressures that decide how hard a market is.

cousins.name: The BCG Matrix
cousins.text: Sorts a company's products into stars, cash cows, question marks and dogs.

cousins.name: The Fishbone Diagram
cousins.text: When a weakness needs fixing, this finds its causes.

grammar.name: must have, might have, can't have
grammar.lead: Detectives — and historians — make guesses about the past from evidence. English uses modal + have + past participle to show how sure we are.
notes:
must have + past participle — you're almost certain something happened.
“The streets are wet. It must have rained in the night.”

might / may / could have + past participle — it's possible.
“I can't find my keys. I might have left them at work.”

can't / couldn't have + past participle — you're almost certain something did NOT happen.
“She can't have seen the message — her phone was switched off.”
Watch out: the opposite of must have is can't have — not mustn't have.
Pronunciation: in speech, have is weak: must've, might've, can't've. Never write “must of”.

exercises.heading: How sure are you?
exercises.intro: Complete with must have, might have or can't have and the verb in brackets.
items: 1. He's got a sun tan. He ___ (be) on holiday. (almost certain)
2. The café is dark. It ___ (close) early — or maybe they're just having a power cut. (possible)
3. She ___ (write) this report — it's full of mistakes, and she's very careful. (almost certain it didn't happen)
4. The team won 5–0. They ___ (play) really well. (almost certain)
5. I don't know where Tom is. He ___ (miss) the train. (possible)

exercises.heading: Detective work: the SWOT mystery
exercises.intro: Use the story. Complete each guess with a modal perfect.
items: 1. Humphrey was on the SOFT team, so he ___ (know) about the idea from the start.
2. The name changed within a few years, so people ___ (find) SOFT hard to use.
3. There were no 1960s documents with Humphrey as the inventor, so he ___ (lead) the project — or there would be some record of it.
answers: 2. might have found (possible — we don't know the reason)

grammar.closing: Now look around you. Make three guesses about what happened here earlier today: one with must have, one with might have, one with can't have.

speak.intro: Put SWOT to work. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “One of our biggest strengths is …” · “An external threat we can't control is …” · “So what? That means we should …” · “It must have been hard to …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Your personal SWOT
paras: Give one strength, one weakness, one opportunity and one threat for your career, studies or English. Then answer: so what?

tasks.label: Task 2 — A place you know
paras: Choose a business, club, school or town you know well. Do a quick SWOT and suggest the first action.

tasks.label: Task 3 — The myth-busters
paras: Tell the story of a “fact” you once believed that turned out to be wrong. How did you find out?

final: Does it matter who invented a tool, as long as it works?
Why do origin stories about one brilliant inventor spread more easily than stories about teams?
Is SWOT too simple for today's fast-changing world? What would you add?
From memory: make three guesses about the SOFT team with must have, might have and can't have.
